scenes.tts: They met in the dissection hall at Prague and recognized each other at once as the same kind of person.

scenes.tts: They married, came to the United States in 1922, and ran headlong into the rules of the era: a Buffalo institute director ordered Gerty to stop publishing with her husband, and she refused; at Washington University she was hired at a tenth of Carl's salary for sixteen years under nepotism rules.

scenes.tts: The lab she built at that salary trained five future Nobel laureates. Working through a fraction everyone else threw away — the supernatant left from recrystallizing phosphorylase — they found the debranching enzyme, and Gerty understood the chromatography spot instantly and ran down the hall shouting, "It's free glucose, it's free glucose!"

scenes.tts: She went further, matching the wrong-shaped glycogen in sick children to a specific missing enzyme: the first proof that one broken enzyme can cause an inherited disease.

scenes.tts: When the Nobel came in 1947, Carl said at the banquet that including his wife was "a source of deep satisfaction to me." He was not being gallant; he was being accurate. The same year, Washington University finally made Gerty a full professor.
